content.confidence: 4: You are confident in your assessment, but not absolutely certain. It is unlikely, but not impossible, that you did not understand some parts of the submission or that you are unfamiliar with some pieces of related work.
content.summary_of_the_paper: This work is on few-shot node classification with graph neural networks. It lifts the requirement for labeled base class data by self-supervised pre-training, it employs a graph transformer and, given a novel task, it learns an additional set of virtual node parameter vectors in the embedding space (prompts), while the backbone is fixed.
content.strength_and_weaknesses:
Pros:
- The paper is very well written in terms of language.
- The method is very simple and makes sense.
- The supervision setting is more realistic than having labeled base class data.
- There are ablations and comparisons with several methods on several datasets.

Cons:
- In the presence of pre-training, the problem formulation is misleading
- Novelty is limited to the application of existing ideas to the particular setting
- There is no discussion or comparison with other works that partially adapt the network
- There is no discussion or comparison with related work on few-shot transductive inference/semi-supervised classification
- Comparisons are unfair concerning the network, maybe also the data

In particular:

Definition 2 (General Few-shot Node Classification) removes base classes from Definition 1 (Traditional Few-shot Node Classification) but says nothing about pre-training. In addition, I could not find anywhere in the experiments or supplementary what data is used for pretraining. If it is the same base class data depending on the dataset, just without the labels, then Definition 2 should say so. If it is other data, again it should specify. In Definition 1, the base class data is used to train the network *from scratch*, and it is not possible to do so on few-shot data alone, as Definition 2 implies. This is misleading.

The novelty is incremental and limited to applying existing ideas to a different setting. In particular:

- Using a graph transformer instead of a traditional graph neural network is not new.
- Unsupervised pre-training with pre-text tasks is also not new.
- Unsupervised pre-training in the context of few-shot learning is also not new.
- Prompts are not new. The main novelty claimed is their application to few-shot node classification, but this incremental. There is no particular challenge to address in this application.

Injecting and learning prompts is a form of partial adaptation of the network where most of the backbone remains fixed, with the objective to address overfitting that would result from full fine-tuning. But there is no discussion or comparison with other such works, for example:

- MAML and other optimization-related methods, where the entire network is fine-tuned but only for a few iterations.
- TADAM and other methods that learn to adapt the data.
- Residual adapters, implanting and other forms of adapting or augmenting the network, while most of it remains fixed.

So the only baselines in the ablation are (1) do not adapt and (2) adapt and overfit by full fine-tuning. This is disregarding all the work done in few-shot learning.

Few-shot node classification is essentially the same problem as few-shot transductive inference, with the only difference in the architecture. Yet the paper does not discuss or compare with related work on few-shot transductive inference or few-shot semi-supervised classification. Again, this is disregarding all the progress made in these settings.

Comparisons in Table 1 are between apples and oranges, because the proposed FS-NPT uses a different backbone than every other method.
content.clarity,_quality,_novelty_and_reproducib:
As detailed above, the language and presentation is of high-quality, but the misleading problem formulation and missing details concerning pre-training data leave the reader wondering what the problem is and what we are comparing.

Also as detailed above, the novelty is limited to applying existing ideas to a different setting.
content.summary_of_the_review: This appears to be a high-quality work but the problem formulation is misleading, the novelty is limited and related work on few-shot learning is not discussed or compared with. Comparisons are unfair.
content.correctness: 4: All of the claims and statements are well-supported and correct.
content.technical_novelty_and_significance: 2: The contributions are only marginally significant or novel.
content.empirical_novelty_and_significance: 2: The contributions are only marginally significant or novel.

content.confidence: 3: You are fairly confident in your assessment. It is possible that you did not understand some parts of the submission or that you are unfamiliar with some pieces of related work. Math/other details were not carefully checked.
content.summary_of_the_paper: The authors propose a prompt-based fine-tuning technique for graph transformers in the context of few-shot node classification. While prompting is a good strategy for fine-tuning language transformers and vision transformers (recently), doing it for graph transformers is not straightforward and the authors address this setting via proposing a new method.
content.strength_and_weaknesses:
Strengths:

	- The setting is realistic, as often you don't have enough samples from the base classes to meta-learn an initialization and in such scenarios leveraging pre-trained models and fine-tuning them is an alternative strategy. This strategy has been a de-facto strategy in vision and language in the recent years.

	- Experimental results are relatively strong as the prompting strategy results in good improvements across the 4 datasets for both 5-shot and 1-shot cases. 

	- Significant analysis and ablations of the proposed method. 


Weakness:
	- [Major]: I have certain reservations about the novelty of the method. The high-level general idea is directly borrowed from the language literature and adapted to the graph transformer. The technical novelty is limited, however I appreciate the authors in verifying that the idea works for graph transformers. It would be beneficial to add some insights early on in the paper, on why designing prompting techniques for graph transformers is challenging.

       - Can the authors provide ablations with different pre-training strategies for graph transformers?
content.clarity,_quality,_novelty_and_reproducib: Although I am not an expert in GNNs, the paper is well-written and has solid clarity.  The primary weakness of the paper is the novelty, as prompting is a well-known method for tuning transformers in general.
content.summary_of_the_review: The authors conduct a good empirical investigation on using prompting for few-shot node classification with supporting ablations. However, the major weakness of the paper is novelty of the method; It's a modification of existing prompting technique applied to graph transformers.  I would be leaning on the side of the weak reject, due to this weakness.
content.correctness: 4: All of the claims and statements are well-supported and correct.
content.technical_novelty_and_significance: 2: The contributions are only marginally significant or novel.
content.empirical_novelty_and_significance: 2: The contributions are only marginally significant or novel.

content.summary_of_the_paper: This paper focuses on the problem of Few-Shot Node Classification (FSNC) and generalize conventional FSNC by removing the assumption that there exist abundant labeled nodes for the base classes. A Few-Shot Node Prompt Tuning method is presented to modulate pretrained Graph Transformers according to different FSNC tasks. Experiments are conducted on four widely used datasets.
content.strength_and_weaknesses:
Strengths:
1. Extensive experiments on the four datasets show the effectiveness of the proposed method.
2. The paper is well written.
Weaknesses:
1. A major concern is the limited novelty. Prompt tuning has been proposed in previous works [A, B] and it seems that the key contribution of the paper is the application to a new task, i.e., few-shot node classification.
A. Visual Prompt Tuning, ECCV2022.
B. The Power of Scale for Parameter-Efficient Prompt Tuning, EMNLP2021. 
2. In Section 4.1, the authors say “It is notable that our method does not have any assumption for base classes, but this assumption is necessary for all the baselines”. Are the base classes necessary for the graph contrastive learning (GCL) methods?
content.clarity,_quality,_novelty_and_reproducib: Please refer to Strengths and Weaknesses.
content.summary_of_the_review: I believe this paper is slightly below the acceptance threshold due to its limited novelty.
